newsitem.title: UK: Adams lauds "momentous" IRA truce decision.
newsitem.headline: Adams lauds "momentous" IRA truce decision.

text.p: Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, praised his guerrilla allies on Saturday for calling a new ceasefire and said it set the stage for negotiations to end decades of Northern Ireland conflict.

Adams and Martin McGuinness, his chief lieutenant, appealed to Unionist politicians who speak for the province's pro-British majority to join with them in talks on a new political settlement that are due to start on September 15.

"In Sinn Fein's view the decision by the IRA (Irish Republican Army) is a momentous one. I want to commend the IRA leadership for having the courage to take that forward-looking decision," Adams told a packed news conference in the heart of Catholic west Belfast.
Hours earlier the IRA, which has waged a 28-year campaign against British rule, announced a "complete cessation of military operations" effective midday Sunday.

In a move acclaimed by British and Irish leaders, the IRA announced that it was restoring a ceasefire that it first called on August 31 1994 and which lasted until February 1996 when its guerrillas set off bombs in London.

It followed assurances by Britain's new Labour government that the "decommissioning" or surrender of IRA arms would not be demanded as a condition to Sinn Fein's entry to the talks but would be handled in parallel with political negotiations.
Adams said the talks offered hope of a settlement and urged the divided pro-British and pro-Irish communities to change ingrained attitudes.

"We have another chance. Let those of us who are charged with political leadership, and that includes the media, build on that chance, educate people about that chance, create the climate were we can have a decommissioning of minds that is required," the Sinn Fein president declared.
Sinn Fein blames the collapse of the last IRA truce on demands by the previous British Conservative government for a handover of guns before Sinn Fein could be admitted to talks.
"Assurances have been given that the issue of decommissioning will not be allowed to block negotiations," Adams said.

He said Britain's Labour Prime Minister Tony Blair, elected to office in May and who has spearheaded attempts to ease the Northern Ireland conflict, had a particular responsibility to make sure the talks reached the goal of a settlement.
"Mr Blair has a responsibility to be part of the partnership for peace which must be brought about and which must be consolidated if we are to have a democratic peace settlement."

McGuinness, like Adams, elected to the British parliament in May elections although both have failed to take their seats, said Northern Ireland should learn the lessons of the peace processes in the Middle East and South Africa.
"We all need to learn those lessons. We all need to declare a ceasefire in our minds," said senior strategist McGuinness.

He urged Unionists not to dwell on the past but to look to the future. Two hardline Unionist parties have hinted that they will boycott the talks but the third, the mainstream Ulster Unionist Party, has yet to show its hand.
"What we need are real negotiations, not useless recriminations," he declared.

"What we are asking the leadership of the Unionist parties is to have confidence in their own abilities and in the people who support them and to come to the negotiating table on September 15 and to sit down with us and work out a resolution to a conflict that has been so much to the detriment of the British and Irish people, of nationalists and of unionists", McGuinness said.
